title: The beginners' orchestra
subtitle: An orchestra in which nobody can play when they join sounds like a terrible idea. Five years on, it has a waiting list.
text: When the conductor James Okoro advertised for members of a new orchestra in Bristol, he added one unusual condition: nobody who could already play an instrument would be accepted. {1} More than two hundred people replied in the first week, ranging in age from nineteen to eighty-four, and he had to borrow a school hall to fit them all in.

Okoro's idea came from his years teaching music in schools. Parents and grandparents would often tell him at concerts that they regretted giving up an instrument as children, or never starting one at all. {2} An orchestra made up entirely of beginners, he reasoned, would remove that fear, because everyone in it would start at the same level.

The first rehearsals were, by everyone's account, painful to listen to. Instruments were borrowed from schools and charities, and many members had never held a violin or a trumpet before. Few of them could read music, and some had never sung in public, let alone played. {3} For the first three months, the orchestra played nothing but single long notes, together, until all eighty players could start and finish at the same moment.

Progress was slow, and around a third of the original members left before the end of the first year. {4} Some of those who stayed say it was the simplest of his rules that kept them going: nobody is ever allowed to apologise for a wrong note, in rehearsal or anywhere else.

The orchestra gave its first public concert after eighteen months, in a church hall with seats for a hundred and fifty. Okoro had worried that the hall would look embarrassingly empty. {5} The programme lasted only twenty-five minutes and included one piece that the orchestra had to start twice. The audience, made up largely of members' friends and families, gave them a standing ovation anyway.

Today the orchestra has ninety members and a waiting list of more than a hundred. Members pay a small fee, and nobody is turned away for being unable to afford it. Several players have gone on to join other amateur groups, and one, a retired dentist who took up the cello at seventy, now plays in a string quartet. {6} Groups based on the same idea have since been set up in four other cities.

Okoro still conducts every rehearsal, and he still accepts only beginners; when players become too good, he gently suggests that they move on to make room for someone new. Asked what he has learned, he says it is something about audiences rather than musicians. 'People don't come to hear us play perfectly,' he says. 'They come to watch us try.'
sentences: Okoro decided that, before they could learn a tune, they had to learn to listen to each other.
Her story was widely reported in the national press.
He had been hoping for perhaps twenty replies.
Those who had played before were asked to help the beginners.
Almost three hundred people turned up, and many had to stand at the back.
When he asked why they did not simply start now, the answer was nearly always the same: they were afraid of being the worst in the room.
Okoro is not troubled by this; in his experience, people who give up an instrument usually do so in the first few months.
why: 'He' is Okoro; twenty is the number he hoped for, and 'more than two hundred' then beats it.
'They' are the parents and grandparents; their fear of 'being the worst in the room' is 'that fear' in the next sentence.
Learning 'to listen to each other' is why they played 'single long notes, together'. D contradicts the opening rule: nobody who could already play was accepted.
'This' is a third of the members leaving; 'some of those who stayed' then turns to the rest.
Three hundred people for a hundred and fifty seats; 'the audience' that stood up is this crowd.
'Her' is the retired dentist; press coverage explains how the idea reached 'four other cities'.
